title: SYSK Selects: How the Deep Web Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of a past episode on the deep web and dark web. Chuck introduces it as a Saturday pick from roughly six years earlier. The hosts explain the deep web as web pages search engines cannot index (password-protected, unlinked, or otherwise hidden), contrast it with the surface web (about 0.03 percent of pages by their figure), and describe search engine crawlers and indexes. Examples include bit torrent sites, government grant databases, online banking pages, and internal company pages. They discuss the dark web as intentionally anonymous sites, the Onion Router (Tor) and .onion domains, the Silk Road case and Ross Ulbricht, the FBI malware operation against Freedom Hosting users, legitimate uses for dissidents and whistleblowers, and companies such as BrightPlanet and Vocative that harvest deep web data. The episode ends with a listener mail birthday shout-out.

segments.title: Selects intro and banter
segments.summary: Chuck introduces this Saturday Selects pick on the deep web. Josh and Chuck banter, and Chuck clarifies that the deep web is not necessarily dark.

segments.title: Iron Maiden pirated-music tour anecdote
segments.summary: Josh tells of Iron Maiden using a company to find where their music was pirated most through BitTorrent sites and building a tour around those regions, with Rio as a guess. The anecdote leads into the point that BitTorrent pages sit in the deep web.

segments.title: Defining the deep web and surface web
segments.summary: The hosts define the deep web as pages not indexed by search engines, such as password-protected, unlinked, or timed pages, and contrast it with the surface web. Examples include grants.gov pages, online banking accounts, Twitter tweets before indexing, and internal company pages.

segments.title: How search engines index the web
segments.summary: The hosts explain that search engines use spiders or crawlers to build an index of URLs, page content, and metadata, so results come from the index rather than a live search of the web. They note that surface search results are shallow and that paywalled research is hard to reach.

segments.title: Size of the deep web and big data
segments.summary: The hosts describe the surface web as about 0.03 percent of pages, with the deep web estimated several hundred times larger. They cite roughly fifty million registered domains and a How Stuff Works page count from Tracy Wilson, and discuss big data as unwieldy data at scale.

segments.title: Dark web, anonymity, and Silk Road
segments.summary: The dark web is described as intentionally hidden and anonymous sites. The hosts note privacy uses, and discuss the Silk Road marketplace, its shutdown, the Ross Ulbricht case, bitcoin seizure questions, and alleged contract killings, plus copycat sites.

segments.title: Tor, .onion sites, and the FBI Freedom Hosting malware
segments.summary: Tor is described as software that routes traffic through many servers and gives access to .onion sites. The hosts describe the FBI hacking Freedom Hosting servers, inserting malware that identified users' hardware addresses and locations, and Firefox fixing the flaw.

segments.title: Tor origins and legitimate uses of the dark web
segments.summary: The hosts say Tor was launched by the US Naval Research Laboratory in 2003 for dissidents and whistleblowers. They describe legitimate uses such as news tip sites, private email and file sharing, and political organizing, and mention a University of Luxembourg study of commonly accessed dark web content.
topics: University of Luxembourg dark web study

segments.title: Deep web harvesting companies and closing
segments.summary: The hosts describe BrightPlanet's deep web harvester used by companies and Vocative's use of it for journalism. They close the episode and point listeners to searching How Stuff Works for more on the deep web.
